common_name: Blanche Ferry Sweet Pea (Pink-and-White Bicolor Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Blanche Ferry, introduced in 1889, is a compact-vined heirloom with distinctive rose-pink-and-white bicolor flowers.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Introduced in 1889 and named for the daughter of the D.M. Ferry seed company's founder, Blanche Ferry bears richly fragrant, bicolor flowers with rose-pink standards and white to pale pink wings, on a somewhat shorter, bushier vine than many other heirloom sweet peas of its era. It remains a favorite among heirloom flower gardeners for its strong scent and old-fashioned charm. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

common_name: Henry Eckford Sweet Pea (Vivid Orange-Scarlet Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Henry Eckford is named for the Scottish breeder who transformed sweet peas from small wild-type flowers into the large, colorful Grandiflora forms of the late 1800s.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Named for the Scottish nurseryman whose decades of breeding work founded the modern Grandiflora sweet pea, Henry Eckford bears vivid, richly fragrant, orange-scarlet flowers on a vigorous, tall-climbing vine, representative of the dramatically larger and more colorful sweet peas Eckford introduced starting in the 1880s. It remains a valued heirloom for gardeners tracing sweet pea breeding history as well as for its strong color and fragrance. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom.

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Dorothy Eckford, introduced around 1901, was long considered the finest pure white sweet pea of its era.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Introduced around the turn of the 20th century and named for a member of the famous Eckford sweet pea breeding family, Dorothy Eckford bears large, richly fragrant, pure white flowers that were considered the finest white sweet pea of its time, on a vigorous, tall-climbing vine. Its clean color and strong scent have kept it a favorite heirloom for cutting gardens ever since. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

common_name: Mrs. Collier Sweet Pea (Fragrant Cream-Yellow Grandiflora Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Mrs. Collier is a classic early-1900s heirloom valued for its soft primrose-cream color, among the best in its class at the time of introduction.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Mrs. Collier is an early-1900s Grandiflora heirloom bearing richly fragrant, soft primrose-cream flowers, one of the better yellow-toned sweet peas of its era at a time when true yellow shades were difficult to breed into the species. Its gentle color pairs well with the more saturated pinks, purples, and reds of other heirloom sweet pea varieties in a mixed cutting garden planting. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.
